before: Say a friend sits with you while you fall apart. Most of us feel better and call them again the next time, and they get a little better at it every time while we don't. So steal some of it. Usually what helped was how they just sat there without trying to fix you. Ten seconds of sitting with yourself like that is good enough for a start, so try it before you call next time.
after: The next section, "Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust", is about loving your little one before they trust you. It introduces their line "Big fuckity whoopty doo. I don't believe you."
brief:
This is a whole short section: a heading and four paragraphs. The first paragraph (the 2 a.m. one) is final and must stay word for word; mark its sentences KEEP.
What the section has to get across (any order, any number of paragraphs):
- The Protector's ordinary acts build your little one's trust (a boundary, a costly no, a dreaded task or money mess, a small promise kept; at the big end, leaving a relationship that keeps wearing down your safety), because soothing with no follow-through sounds like the old unreliability.
- The inside half: keeping a surge of fear, rage, craving or shame from running what you say, send, spend or take, or who you sleep with or commit to.
- Some protecting happens between you and your little one (not snapping back at their sarcasm, letting them distrust you, admitting a fair complaint, repairing after you attack yourself), and they see it. Not retaliating is evidence of love but doesn't replace it.
- If the Nurturer isn't there yet, the Protector can go first: a locked door, a meal, a cancelled obligation; warmth later.
- Pick one act and make it specific (when, smallest first step, what help); rehearse a hard moment you can see coming; afterward look honestly at what happened, and keep what helps, not what earns a tick.
Limits: "your little one" is the inner child; never "the kid". Don't invent facts about the author's life.
